title: The four phrases
hook: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease

segments.voice: Yesterday, the camp 2 close: the whole life, from the palace to the sal trees. Your line was you know him now. Did you retell a story to someone? Day ninety-seven, and camp three, the practices, begins.

For seventy-five days you've listened to stories. Now the path turns, and for the next sixty days it's about doing: the sitting, the walking, the precepts, the giving, the chanting, the holy days. And it starts where your very first word started, all the way back on day one: metta, loving-kindness. Back then it was a word. Now it gets hands and feet. Because metta, in most Buddhist schools, isn't only a feeling you wait for. It's something people practice, on purpose, with words, again and again, the way you'd practice a scale on a piano.
screen: `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICE.` → `BACK TO THE FIRST WORD: METTA.` → `PRACTICED LIKE A SCALE.`

segments.voice: Here are the four phrases many meditation centers use today. May you be safe. May you be happy. May you be healthy. May you live with ease. Each one is a wish, not a demand. Safe: free from danger, inside and out. Happy: a settled gladness, not a party. Healthy: in body and mind. At ease: life not being a constant struggle. Now, an honest note. These exact four lines are modern. Teachers in Burma, Thailand and the West shaped phrases like these in the last century, and every center words them a little differently. What's old is the wish itself. The Metta Sutta, one of the most chanted texts in the Theravada world, wishes that all beings be happy and secure, that their hearts be glad. The old manuals, like Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification from the fifth century, give phrases too. So the phrases are a tool, like a handrail. They give the mind something to lean on when the feeling isn't there yet. And that's the part people find surprising: you don't have to feel warm to begin. You say the words slowly and sincerely, and you notice what happens. Some days, warmth. Some days, nothing. Some days, resistance. All of it counts. Over the next ten days you'll send these wishes out in widening circles: to yourself, a helper, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, and finally everyone. Today, just learn the four lines. The last one is your carry.
screen: `SAFE, HAPPY, HEALTHY, AT EASE.` · `THE WORDS ARE MODERN.` · `THE WISH IS OLD.` · `A HANDRAIL, NOT A FEELING.` · then, large: `MAY YOU BE AT EASE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle for a few moments. Now, silently and slowly, say the four phrases once. May you be safe. Pause, and breathe. May you be happy. Pause. May you be healthy. Pause. May you live with ease. Don't aim them at anyone yet. Just let the words be there, and notice what they do in the body: softening, nothing, a little resistance. Whatever shows up is fine. When the words are done, rest in the quiet after them. The bell holds the time.
The four phrases. May you be safe, happy, healthy, and at ease: a modern handrail for the old practice of metta.
Your line: may you be at ease. Today, say it silently once to someone you pass. No need for them to know. Day ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice metta by repeating short wishes, silently or aloud, for themselves and others; the wording varies by teacher and school, and Theravada communities often chant the Metta Sutta itself.

what a scholar hears: metta comes from mitta, a friend; the four-line formula is a twentieth-century teaching form, while the Pali texts and the Visuddhimagga give their own wordings of the wish.
